questions.stem: A charge nurse is told that a single fixed nurse-to-patient ratio can be used for every medical-surgical shift regardless of acuity. Which response best reflects the federal CMS hospital nursing-services requirement?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Federal rules prescribe one identical numerical RN-to-patient ratio for every adult acute-care unit, so acuity and immediate nursing needs do not alter staffing.","B":"Federal rules require only one registered nurse somewhere in the hospital, while the remainder of bedside staffing may be determined without regard to patient need.","C":"Federal rules prohibit licensed practical nurses and other nursing personnel from contributing to hospital staffing when registered nurses are present on the unit.","D":"Hospitals must have adequate licensed nurses and other personnel to meet patient needs, with supervisory and staff coverage ensuring RN availability when needed."}}
questions.rationale: CMS hospital nursing-services requirements do not establish one universal federal numerical ratio for every unit. They require adequate numbers of licensed RNs, LPN/LVNs, and other personnel to provide nursing care to all patients as needed, including staffing that ensures immediate RN availability for bedside care when necessary.
questions.source_detail: Federal hospital requirements call for adequate numbers of nursing personnel based on patient needs and RN availability when needed, not one nationwide fixed ratio.

questions.stem: A trauma client has major external blood loss, heart rate 132/min, blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg, cool clammy skin, and weak peripheral pulses. Which shock pattern is most consistent with these findings?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypovolemic shock, because major blood loss reduces circulating volume and produces compensatory tachycardia, vasoconstriction, and poor peripheral perfusion.","B":"Neurogenic shock, because acute loss of sympathetic tone typically causes marked peripheral vasoconstriction, cool skin, and compensatory tachycardia.","C":"Anaphylactic shock, because systemic mediator release after blood loss characteristically causes cool clammy skin without an allergic trigger or airway findings.","D":"Cardiogenic shock, because hemorrhage primarily causes acute pump failure and pulmonary congestion rather than a reduction in effective circulating volume."}}
questions.rationale: Major hemorrhage reduces effective circulating volume and can produce hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, weak pulses, and impaired perfusion, which is the classic physiology of hypovolemic shock. The history and examination do not support neurogenic, anaphylactic, or primary cardiogenic shock.
questions.source_name: Merck Manual Professional — Overview of Thoracic Trauma / Shock in Trauma
questions.source_detail: Trauma with significant hemorrhage can cause hypovolemic shock; immediate trauma assessment distinguishes hemorrhagic shock from other shock states.

questions.stem: Three days after major trauma, a client develops acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with new bilateral lung opacities that are not primarily explained by cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings most strongly indicate isolated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because bilateral new opacities are not part of an acute inflammatory lung-injury pattern.","B":"The findings are compatible with acute respiratory distress syndrome when required oxygenation and respiratory-support criteria are also satisfied in the clinical setting.","C":"The findings establish cardiogenic pulmonary edema because bilateral opacities in acute respiratory failure are presumed hydrostatic regardless of the clinical context.","D":"The findings exclude acute respiratory distress syndrome because trauma is not recognized as a precipitating risk factor in the current global ARDS framework."}}
questions.rationale: The current Global Definition describes ARDS as acute hypoxemic respiratory failure from inflammatory lung injury after a predisposing risk factor such as trauma, with bilateral opacities and edema not primarily explained by cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Formal classification also depends on oxygenation and respiratory-support criteria; bilateral opacities alone are insufficient.
questions.source_name: Global ARDS Definition Consensus — A New Global Definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.source_detail: Global ARDS framework includes trauma as a risk factor, acute hypoxemia, bilateral opacities, and noncardiogenic inflammatory lung edema, with oxygenation/support criteria for classification.

questions.stem: Several days after abdominal surgery, a client develops abrupt severe abdominal pain, fever, involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, and a rigid abdomen. Which interpretation requires the most urgent escalation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Expected postoperative ileus, because abdominal rigidity and rebound tenderness commonly appear while bowel motility is returning after uncomplicated surgery.","B":"Uncomplicated constipation, because severe pain and fever can be observed until normal bowel movements resume after anesthesia and opioid exposure.","C":"Peritoneal irritation from a possible perforation or other intra-abdominal emergency, requiring immediate surgical evaluation rather than routine observation.","D":"Simple incisional pain, because rebound tenderness is a superficial wound finding that does not suggest inflammation inside the peritoneal cavity."}}
questions.rationale: Rigid involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, severe abdominal pain, and fever are peritoneal signs that can accompany perforation or another acute intra-abdominal process. These findings require urgent evaluation rather than attribution to routine ileus, constipation, or superficial incisional discomfort.
questions.source_name: Merck Manual Professional — Acute Abdominal Pain
questions.source_detail: Peritoneal signs such as involuntary guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness raise concern for a surgical abdominal emergency.

questions.stem: A client with a T4 spinal cord injury suddenly develops a pounding headache, facial flushing, profuse sweating above the lesion, and blood pressure 210/120 mm Hg. Which nursing action is the priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the client flat and elevate the legs because the primary problem is loss of vascular tone with severe hypotension from the high spinal cord injury.","B":"Administer routine analgesia and reassess in one hour because headache and sweating are expected chronic manifestations after an injury above T6.","C":"Encourage the client to bear down and increase abdominal pressure because autonomic dysreflexia is usually relieved by increasing stimulation below the lesion.","D":"Sit the client upright, rapidly assess for triggers such as bladder or bowel distention, monitor blood pressure closely, and escalate emergency management."}}
questions.rationale: The presentation is classic for autonomic dysreflexia, a potentially life-threatening hypertensive emergency in people with spinal cord injury, commonly at or above T6. Immediate management includes upright positioning, frequent blood-pressure monitoring, and rapid identification and removal of triggers, especially bladder or bowel problems.
questions.source_name: Paralyzed Veterans of America / Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine — Autonomic Dysreflexia CPG
questions.source_detail: Current PVA clinical guidance addresses prompt recognition and management of autonomic dysreflexia and common triggering stimuli after spinal cord injury.
